history: Founded in 919 over the tomb of Sugawara no Michizane, the Heian scholar-statesman who died in exile at Dazaifu in 903. After misfortunes struck the capital, he was deified as Tenjin, the kami of learning.
why_visit: The spiritual home of students across Japan, who come to pray for academic success; the grounds are famed for some 6,000 plum trees that bloom in late winter.
prayer_focus: Academic achievement (学業成就) and success in examinations (合格祈願), petitioned on ema and at the bronze ox statues.
best_season: Late February to March for the plum blossoms (Michizane's beloved flower); examination season draws the largest crowds.

history: Founded in 711 on Inariyama, the shrine is the origin of the nationwide Inari faith. Its hillside paths are lined with thousands of torii donated by worshippers and businesses in gratitude for prosperity.
why_visit: The Senbon Torii — corridors of vermilion gates winding up the sacred mountain — are among the most recognizable sights in Japan, and the four-kilometer mountain circuit passes countless smaller shrines and stone foxes.
prayer_focus: Abundant harvest (五穀豊穣), prosperity in business (商売繁盛), and household fortune. Fox (kitsune) statues serve as the messengers of Inari.
best_season: Year-round; especially atmospheric at dawn and during the February Hatsuuma festival and autumn foliage.

history: Traditionally said to date to the reign of Emperor Korei. The shrine gave its name to the district of Omiya ('great shrine') and was designated the ichinomiya of Musashi Province. Its 2km approach (sando) is among the longest in Japan.
why_visit: The central Hikawa shrine of the Kanto region and the source of the Hikawa network's worship of Susanoo. The long tree-lined approach and the vermilion Romon gate make it a serene retreat within greater Tokyo.
prayer_focus: Matchmaking and good marriage (縁結び), warding off misfortune, and family safety.
best_season: Early summer for fresh greenery along the approach; the August Reitaisai festival.

history: Of mythic antiquity, the shrine is tied in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki to the kuni-yuzuri, the ceding of the land by Okuninushi to the heavenly deities, in return for which the great shrine was built.
why_visit: The towering honden and the colossal shimenawa rope of the Kagura-den make Izumo unforgettable; it is the foremost shrine of enmusubi, the binding of good relationships.
prayer_focus: Matchmaking and good relationships (縁結び), good marriage, and fortune.
best_season: The 10th lunar month — known elsewhere as Kannazuki (month without gods) but at Izumo as Kamiarizuki, the month the gods gather here.

history: Established in 1920 to enshrine the spirits of Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, set within an artificial evergreen forest designed to mature over centuries.
why_visit: One of Japan's most visited shrines, drawing millions for hatsumode, and a tranquil expanse of woodland minutes from Harajuku.
prayer_focus: Family harmony (家内安全), peace of the nation, and the fulfillment of heartfelt wishes, often written on ema beneath the great camphor trees.
best_season: New Year for hatsumode; fresh green in early summer; the November autumn festival.

history: Founded in the 7th century as Gion-sha, the shrine became the cult center of the Gion faith that arose to placate epidemics. It was renamed Yasaka Shrine in 1868 during the Meiji separation of Buddhism and Shinto (shinbutsu bunri).
why_visit: The head shrine of roughly 2,300 Yasaka/Gion shrines nationwide and the spiritual home of the Gion Matsuri, one of Japan's three great festivals. Its vermilion West Gate above Shijo-dori is a defining Kyoto landmark.
prayer_focus: Protection from epidemics and misfortune (厄除け yakuyoke), prosperity in business (商売繁盛), and good fortune.
best_season: July for the Gion Matsuri; cherry blossoms in adjacent Maruyama Park in early April; lantern-lit evenings year-round.
